background.definition: Hairy cell leukemia is a chronic B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder with a characteristic presentation of pancytopenia, splenomegaly, and circulating lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections.

list.listitem: There are about 3 cases per 1,000,000 people in the United States per year.
It represents about 2% of new diagnoses of leukemia, which equates to about 1250 new cases per year.
There is a male predominance of about 4 to 1. HCL has an increased incidence in whites, but a decreased incidence in Africans, Arabs, and Asians.
The median age of diagnosis is 58 years.
No specific etiologic agent has been firmly established.
Exposure to pesticides, petroleum products, and ionizing radiation has been reported to increase the risk of developing HCL.
HCL is an indolent lymphoproliferative disorder that typically infiltrates the bone marrow and the spleen.
The bone marrow infiltration limits adequate production of red blood cells, platelets, and monocytes.
The bone marrow typically has an increase in reticulin fibers, which leads to a fibrotic bone marrow.
HCL exhibits a characteristic immunophenotypic profile that is positive for the B-cell markers CD11c, CD19, CD20, CD22, CD25 CD103, CD123, and CD200. Expression of Annexin A1 is very specific to HCL.
Over 85% of patients with HCL will exhibit IGHV genes with somatic hypermutation.

The BRAF V600E mutation is characteristic of HCL and development of the VE1 antibody offers a surrogate marker for this mutation using immunohistochemistry. This enables high senstivity and specificity in diagnosing HCL.
The abnormal lymphocytes have increased enzymatic activity of tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), which was used in the past to make the diagnosis.
Due to the leukopenias from this condition, these patients are susceptible to infections, including the opportunistic infections.
Obtain a peripheral smear to evaluate for abnormal lymphocytes with fine, hair-like projections in a patient who presents with pancytopenia and splenomegaly. C
A bone marrow biopsy is required to make the diagnosis; a "dry tap" is commonly seen in this condition, due to fibrosis created by the abnormal cells. B
The cells should express the B-cell markers CD19, CD20, CD22, as well as CD103, CD11c, CD123, CD200 and CD25. The cells should also be negative for CD5, CD10, and CD23. C

Differential.Differential_Features: HCLv typically with leukocytosis, no monocytopenia, CD25 and CD123 negative, BRAF V600E negative
B cells for CLL are usually CD5 and CD23 positive
Typically elevated lymphocyte count with over 55% morphologically appearing prolymphocytes

list.listitem: Fatigue is a common presenting symptom (80%) Other symptoms include fevers, night sweats, left upper quadrant abdominal pain from splenomegaly, and bruising.
Infections are also seen due to leukopenia.
Common clinical features include splenomegaly (60%-70%), hepatomegaly (40%-50%), and abdominal lymph node enlargement on CT (10%).
Asymptomatic patients can be identified when a CBC is done for other reasons, or if splenomegaly is found incidentally on physical examination.
Anemia is seen in about 70% of patients, thrombocytopenia in 80%, and leukopenia in 65%.
The peripheral smear demonstrates circulating atypical lymphocytes with circumferential cytoplasmic projections, called hairy cells in 95% of patients.
Monocytopenia is a found in almost all case of HCL.
Bone marrow biopsy is essential for the diagnosis of HCL. A dry tap is commonly seen in this condition, due to fibrosis created by the abnormal cells.

Immunophenotyping is necessary to identify the co-expression of CD19, CD20, CD103, CD22, CD25, CD11c, CD123, CD200, and Annexin A1 with a typical B-cell clonal pattern and to make a differential diagnosis from other indolent malignancies. The cells should also be negative for CD5, CD10, and CD23.

Cytochemical TRAP staining is usually positive on both the peripheral smear and bone marrow aspirate (if an aspirate can be obtained). However, due to technical challenges, this cytochemical stain has been replaced with immunohistochemistry techniques. The latter was 81% sensitive with 100% positive predictive value and 82% negative predictive value compared with flow cytometry in a series of 148 patients.
Patients should have an analysis for the BRAF mutation using a sensitive molecular assay, such as PCR or next generation sequencing.
Consider doing molecular analysis for the IGHV4-34 rearrangement, which is found in BRAF negative patients, who have anHCL variant.
In patients with splenomegaly, order a CBC and if cytopenia is present, order a peripheral smear.

If the hair-like projections are seen on the lymphocytes, consider HCL. Review of the smear can also help determine whether immature cells are present, which could represent another hematologic abnormality.
To confirm the diagnosis, a bone marrow is required, with appropriate immunophenotyping or flow cytometry on the bone marrow aspirate and biopsy required.
Consensus guidelines recommend obtaining a complete metabolic profile and lactate dehyrogenase. In addition, Hepatitis B and C testing is suggested if treatment with rituximab is to be added.
Observe asymptomatic patients. B
Treatment is indicated only when the patient has a significant cytopenia, recurrent infections, marked constitutional symptoms (such as fatigue, fever, or night sweats), or massive splenomegaly. C
The combination of cladribine + rituximab can be considered for first line therapy. A
Pentostatin (2'-deoxycoformcyin) and cladrabine (2-chlorodeoxyadenosine) are purine analogs that have conclusively been shown to induce durable remissions in most patients. A

Treatment is indicated only when the disease is considered "active." Active disease is present when the patient has a significant cytopenia, recurrent infections, marked constitutional symptoms (such as fatigue, fever, or night sweats), or massive splenomegaly. Significant cytopenias are defined by a hemoglobin <11 gm/dL, platelet count <100,000/μL, and/or a neutrophil count <1,000 μL.

Pentostatin and cladrabine are purine analogues that target the lymphocytes and are cytotoxic to both resting and dividing cells. Both of these agents induce durable complete remissions in most patients.

In a series of 185 patients treated with pentostatin, 81% had a complete response, with a median disease-free survival of 15 years. Among 34 patients treated with cladrabine, the complete response rate was 82%, and the disease-free survival was over 11 years. These regimens are relatively well tolerated, with low incidence of serious adverse effects.

A study randomized 68 patients being treated with cladribine to immediate or delayed (>6 months) rituximab. At 96 months 94% versus 12% in the placebo group remained free of minimal residual disease. Due to these results, the combination of cladribine + rituximab can be considered for first line therapy.
In the event of relapse, retreatment with pentostatin or cladribine (or use of the alternative agent) is often successful with or without the addition of rituximab.
In a small series of 8 patients, the combination of purine analogs with rituximab was safe and effective for patients with recurrent or refractory HCL (87% complete remission).

Moxetumomab pasudotox, a recombinant immunotoxin targeting CD22, has been FDA approved for relapsed HCL, in patients who have received at least 2 prior systemic therapies, including a purine nucleside analog.

Early trials suggest that BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib can achieve significant responses (overall response rate of 100% with 35%-40% complete remissions); however, the duration of those responses was relatively short (19 months for those with a complete response and 6 months for those with a partial response). More investigation is required before the common use of these medications is recommended.

In a series of 30 patients with relapsed or refractory HCL, they were given the combination of vemurafenib 960 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, as well as sequential rituximab given in 8 doses over 18 weeks. A complete response was seen in 26 of 30 patients, including among those previously treated with a BRAF inhibitor.

For those patients relapsing within 5 years of initial therapy the use of novel agents might be considered and there are now a number of series published using BRAF inhibitors alone and in combination.
Splenectomy was the first effective therapy for HCL and can induce remissions in over 40% of patients.
Splenectomy may be still indicated in patients with massive, symptomatic splenomegaly.
Prior to the advent of effective therapy, the 5- and 10-year survival rates of untreated patients were 34.4% and 29.6%, respectively. B
Patients with HCL now have an excellent prognosis due to the indolent nature and the efficacy of treatment, with overall survival at 10 years of over 95%. B
In a series of 203 patients from 12 Israeli medical centers, 5 and 10 year survival were 96% and 91%.

Patients with HCL are at increased risk of a second cancer (standardized incidence ratio [SIR] 1.24). Risk is greatest for Hodgkin's lymphoma (SIR 6.6), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (SIR 5.0), and thyroid cancer (SIR 3.6). B

At follow-up visits, ask about fatigue, bleeding symptoms, infections, and abdominal fullness and obtain a CBC. Frequency depends on the patients' symptoms, how long they have had the disease, and any recent changes in laboratory values. C
